t: Saadat Ali Khan I, appointed Subahdar of Oudh in 1722, subdued local powers and consolidated Oudh as a state as Mughal authority declined.
The East India Company's victory at the Battle of Buxar in 1764 began a long period of British interference, subsidies and cessions of land.
Lord Dalhousie deposed Wajid Ali Shah and annexed Oudh on 7 February 1856, on the grounds of alleged misrule; Oudh rose against British rule in the rebellion of 1857.
dyk: Ghazi-ud-Din Haidar Shah instituted the Oudh Bequest, fixed payments by the British to the Shia holy cities of Najaf and Karbala, paid as interest on a loan Oudh made to the Company in 1825.
ev: Saadat Ali Khan I is appointed Subahdar of Oudh Subah and subdues the Shaikhzadas of Lucknow and Raja Mohan Singh of Tiloi
Saadat Khan leads Oudh's forces against Nader Shah's invasion and is captured at the Battle of Karnal
Safdar Jang gains the subah of Allahabad, arguably the zenith of Oudh's territorial span
The East India Company defeats Shuja-ud-Daula and Mir Kasim at the Battle of Buxar
At the end of the First Rohilla War Oudh gains the whole of Rohilkhand and the Middle Doab
Saadat Ali Khan II cedes Rohilkhand, the Lower Doab and Gorakhpur to the British, halving the state
Ghazi-ud-Din Haidar Shah takes the title of Badshah (king), signalling formal independence from the Mughal Empire
Lord Dalhousie deposes Wajid Ali Shah and annexes Oudh to the East India Company's territories

f.capital: Ayodhya, then Faizabad (from 1740); the Company's Residents sat at Lucknow
f.founder: Saadat Ali Khan I, appointed Subahdar of Oudh in 1722
f.predecessor: Oudh Subah of the Mughal Empire
f.successor: North Western Provinces and Oudh (British India)
